textTitles: Staff car park: permits and rules

paragraphs.text: Riverside Community Choir — new members welcome. We are a mixed choir of about sixty singers and we rehearse every Thursday from 7.30 pm to 9.30 pm in the main hall of Riverside Primary School, during school term only. There is no audition. You do not need to read music, although it helps, and our musical director teaches every part by ear before we look at the written score. New members may join at any rehearsal before the end of October or after the winter concert in January.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Membership costs £45 a term, paid in the first three weeks; students and anyone receiving unemployment benefit pay half. Your first two rehearsals are free, so that you can decide whether the choir suits you before paying anything. Printed music is lent to members and must be returned at the end of each term in the folder it came in; a lost copy is charged at £5. We perform twice a year, at Christmas and in early summer, and members are expected to attend at least three of the last four rehearsals before a concert.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: To join, simply turn up on a Thursday and speak to the membership secretary at the table by the door, who will ask which part you would like to sing and take your contact details. Please arrive by 7.15 on your first evening so there is time to find you a seat in the right section. Tea and biscuits are served at the break for a small donation.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Junior Sports Camp (ages 7–11). Five full days a week, 9 am to 4 pm, throughout the summer holiday. Children try a different sport each day, including football, tennis, gymnastics and swimming, and finish the week with a mini sports day to which parents are invited. Bring a packed lunch and a refillable water bottle. £22 a day or £95 for a full week; places can be booked for single days.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Art Studio (ages 8–13). Mornings only, 9.30 am to 12.30 pm, Monday to Thursday. Each week has a theme, and young artists work with paint, clay and printing to produce a finished piece they can take home on Thursday. All materials are provided, but children should wear old clothes, as paint does not always wash out. Places must be booked for a whole week, at £60.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Little Explorers (ages 4–6). A gentle introduction to holiday clubs for younger children, with outdoor games, stories and simple crafts. Sessions run on Tuesdays and Fridays from 10 am to 12 noon, and a parent or carer must stay on site throughout, although not in the room. £8 per session; no booking is needed, but numbers are limited to twenty, so arrive early.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Teen Leaders (ages 14–16). For young people who would like experience of working with children. Participants help to run the Junior Sports Camp for two weeks and receive a certificate that can be included in job and college applications. There is no charge, but places are limited to eight and applicants must attend a short interview in June.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: C
texts.title: Staff car park: permits and rules

paragraphs.text: Staff car park: permits and rules. The car park behind the main building has 140 spaces for around 400 staff, so a permit does not guarantee a space and parking is on a first-come, first-served basis. Permits are issued by the facilities team and are free, but they are allocated according to need. Priority goes to staff with a disability, those who work shifts starting before 7 am or finishing after 9 pm, and those who live more than ten miles away with no reasonable public transport route.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Apply using the form on the staff intranet and attach a copy of your vehicle registration document. Applications are reviewed on the first working day of each month, and permits are posted to your department. Each permit covers up to two vehicles, but only one may be parked at a time. If you change your vehicle, tell the facilities team within a week so that the record can be updated; the barrier cameras read number plates, and an unregistered car will not be let in.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Inside the car park the speed limit is 5 miles per hour, and vehicles must be reversed into bays so that they can leave quickly in an emergency. The row nearest the entrance is reserved for visitors and must not be used by staff at any time, even when it is empty. Charging points for electric vehicles are in the far corner; a car must be moved once it is fully charged, and in any case after four hours.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Staff who park in breach of these rules receive a written warning. A second breach within twelve months means the permit is withdrawn for three months. Anyone who does not need to drive every day is encouraged to use the cycle shelter, which has showers nearby, or the car-sharing scheme, whose members are guaranteed a space if they arrive together before 9 am. The facilities team reviews all permits every April.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Requesting flexible working. Any employee who has completed six months’ continuous service may ask for a change to their working pattern, whether to their hours, the times they work or the place they work from. Examples include compressed hours, where the same total is worked over fewer days, a later start and finish, or working from home on set days. You may make one request in any twelve-month period.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Put your request in writing to your line manager, using the form on the intranet. Explain the change you would like, the date you would like it to start and how you think any effect on your team could be managed. You do not have to give a reason for the request, although many staff find that explaining their circumstances helps the discussion. Requests are considered in the order in which they are received, and a manager who receives several at once may look at them together to see how the team as a whole would be affected.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Your manager will arrange a meeting within four weeks of receiving the form and may invite someone from human resources. You may bring a colleague with you. A decision will be given in writing within two weeks of the meeting. If the request is accepted, the new pattern is a permanent change to your contract unless a trial period has been agreed; trials normally last three months and are reviewed at the end. A trial can be ended early by either side with two weeks’ notice.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A request can be refused only for a business reason, such as the cost of the change, an effect on customers that cannot be avoided, or an inability to reorganise work among other staff, and the letter must say which reason applies. If you disagree with the decision you may appeal within ten days to a manager who was not involved in the original meeting. The outcome of the appeal is final.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The queue is one of the most ordinary features of modern life and one of the least examined. Few everyday institutions reveal so much about how strangers manage to share limited resources without an argument. People join one at a bus stop, a post office or a ticket office without thinking about it, obey rules that nobody has written down, and feel real anger when those rules are broken. Yet orderly queuing is neither universal nor very old. In many places and periods, the normal way to get served was to push to the front, and the idea that people should wait in a line in the order they arrived had to be learned.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Historians usually trace the modern queue to the growth of cities in the nineteenth century, when large numbers of strangers began to need the same service at the same time. A baker in a village knew every customer and could serve them in whatever order local custom required; a railway ticket office in a city of a million people could not. The line, in which each person’s position depends only on the time of arrival, solved a problem that personal knowledge could no longer solve. It is, in that sense, a technology for dealing fairly with people one does not know.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Wartime rationing turned queuing into a national habit in several countries. When basic goods were scarce and distributed in fixed quantities, waiting in line became a daily task, and newspapers of the period are full of complaints about the hours spent in it. Some historians argue that the association between queuing and fairness was strengthened by this experience, since the queue made scarcity visible and seemed to share it equally. Others point out that the queues of that period were also places of conflict, where accusations of pushing in were common and occasionally ended in the courts. The habit outlasted the shortages, and in some places the queue came to be regarded as a matter of national pride.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Psychologists who study queues have found that the experience of waiting matters as much as its length. People consistently overestimate how long they have waited, and they tolerate a long wait better when they know how long it will be, when they can see progress, and when they believe the wait is fair. A single line that feeds several counters is generally preferred to separate lines for each counter, even when the average wait is the same, because it removes the frustration of watching a neighbouring line move faster. Many banks and airports adopted the single line for this reason. Airlines found that walking passengers a longer distance to the baggage hall reduced complaints about waiting at the carousel, although the total time was unchanged.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Fairness, it turns out, is the rule people care about most. In experiments where someone pushes into a queue, the people directly behind the intruder are most likely to object, but those further back often object too, even though the intrusion costs them only a few seconds. The strength of the reaction suggests that people are defending a principle rather than their own time. Interestingly, an intruder who offers a reason, even a weak one, meets less resistance than one who says nothing, a finding that has been repeated in several countries.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Technology has changed where queues happen without removing them. Telephone systems place callers in a virtual line and announce their position; online shops release popular items at a fixed time and form queues of thousands of people who never see one another; theme parks sell tickets that allow visitors to skip a line for a fee. These arrangements raise questions that the physical queue avoided. A paid right to skip the line is openly unequal, and a virtual queue that cannot be seen is harder to trust, since nobody can check that it is being run fairly. Some companies now publish how their virtual queues work in order to reassure customers.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Not all societies treat the queue in the same way, but the differences are often exaggerated. Popular accounts describe certain nationalities as naturally orderly and others as naturally disorderly, yet observational studies find that behaviour depends heavily on the situation: people who queue patiently at a bus stop may crowd a counter when the service is chaotic, and people from supposedly disorderly places form perfect lines when a clear system is provided. What looks like national character is frequently a response to how well the waiting is organised. The same crowd can behave very differently on different days.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The queue, then, is less a matter of temperament than of design. It works when the rules are clear, when progress is visible and when people trust that the order will be respected, and it breaks down when any of those conditions fails. Organisations that manage waiting well tend to pay as much attention to these conditions as to reducing the wait itself, because a short wait that feels unfair generates more complaints than a long one that feels just. The line at the post office is, in its modest way, a daily lesson in how strangers agree to cooperate.
paragraphs.label: H
